text: In our social-cognitive framework, a narrative is the organized story form people use to link personal episodes into a meaningful arc, allowing experiences to be remembered and communicated as ‘what happened, why it mattered, and what it led to.’ (p. 12)
text_normalised: A narrative is an organized story-like structure that connects events into a meaningful arc. It helps individuals interpret experiences by linking what occurred to its significance and perceived consequences. Narratives support memory, sense-making, and communication by turning episodes into coherent accounts.

text: We define narrative as a shared interpretive template that a group uses to explain its situation: it identifies key actors, assigns motives, and indicates what outcomes are likely or desirable. (p. 13)
text_normalised: A narrative is a shared interpretive template used by a group to explain a situation. It highlights relevant actors, attributes motives, and sketches expected or preferred outcomes. Narratives guide collective understanding by organizing social information into an intelligible account.

text: From an identity perspective, narratives are self-defining storylines: they select particular memories, arrange them in sequence, and thereby stabilize ‘who I am’ across changing contexts. (p. 44)
text_normalised: Narratives are self-defining storylines that select and arrange memories to support a stable sense of identity. By sequencing experiences, narratives help people maintain continuity of self across contexts and time.

text: In interpersonal settings, narrative is a conversational accomplishment. Speakers build a plot in interaction, invite the listener into a stance, and negotiate what the account means for the relationship. (p. 7)
text_normalised: A narrative is an interactional product constructed in conversation. It involves building a plot, positioning the teller and listener, and negotiating the relational meaning of the account. Narratives function as social actions, not only as content.

text: Narratives can be treated as cultural scripts: publicly available story patterns that prescribe what counts as a ‘normal’ sequence of events and what emotions are appropriate at each stage. (p. 9)
text_normalised: A narrative is a cultural script that provides widely shared story patterns. It specifies expected sequences of events and culturally appropriate emotional responses. Narratives shape judgments by defining what seems normal, deviant, or justified.

text: We use the term narrative for causal stories of inequality—accounts that explain why some groups are advantaged and others are not, and that imply who should be blamed, helped, or resisted. (p. 203)
text_normalised: A narrative is a causal story that explains social outcomes such as inequality. It frames why disparities exist and implies responsibility, blame, deservingness, and appropriate responses. Narratives influence attitudes by shaping moral evaluation and policy preferences.

text: A narrative is not merely a timeline; it is an evaluative ordering. People highlight some events, omit others, and attach lessons, thereby making the sequence persuasive to themselves and to audiences. (p. 31)
text_normalised: A narrative is an evaluative ordering of events rather than a simple chronology. It involves selection, emphasis, omission, and lesson-drawing. Narratives can persuade by presenting a sequence as meaningful and normatively interpretable.

text: In studies of collective memory, narrative refers to the community-level story that anchors commemorations: it provides a beginning, a turning point, and a moral that can be ritually repeated. (p. 88)
text_normalised: A narrative is a community-level story that structures collective memory. It organizes the past around key moments and a moral interpretation that can be reiterated in commemorations. Narratives help groups maintain a shared understanding of history.

text: We define narrative as an emotion-guiding account that names a threat, identifies a protector, and outlines a path from fear to safety, thereby coordinating group feelings and action. (p. 5)
text_normalised: A narrative is an emotion-guiding account that frames a situation in terms of threat, protection, and a pathway to safety or resolution. It coordinates group emotions and can motivate collective action by linking feelings to an implied course of behavior.

text: Within attribution research, narratives are explanatory bundles: people connect situational cues and dispositions into a story that ‘makes sense’ of behavior, even when evidence is incomplete. (p. 62)
text_normalised: A narrative is an explanatory bundle that integrates cues into a coherent story about behavior. It links situational and dispositional elements to create sense-making under uncertainty. Narratives can fill gaps in evidence by providing plausible connections among events and motives.
